extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting effective dialogue in fiction: how to render realistic-sounding speech that also advances character, subtext, and story. Covers conventions (punctuation, tags), techniques (stage directions, indirect dialogue), pitfalls (exposition, overdone dialect), and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to real speech to develop an ear for dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to get a feel for realistic dialogue is by listening to people talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen to people on the bus, in the elevator, on the radio; pay attention to their speech patterns and the content of their conversations. Imagine writing their words down or actually transcribe conversations to develop your ear. Being able to listen and mimic is the best preparation for writing realistic dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contractions in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractions are good; most folks speak with contractions rather than full forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only a very formal person would say 'I do not think this is the best idea.' Most would say 'I don't think this is the best idea.' Use contractions to make speech sound natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow characters to use clichés when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Though writers are instructed to avoid clichés, characters often use hackneyed phrasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a description, 'hot as hell' may do little, but certain characters might reasonably use such phrases; allow clichéd turns of phrase if they fit character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue must be more focused and significant than real speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional dialogue needs to have more impact, focus, and relevance than ordinary conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real-life conversations are often dull or meandering; on the page dialogue should get to the point faster and serve narrative/character needs. Avoid transcribing mundane filler unless it serves a purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elide dull filler; make dialogue concise
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut the 'ums', repeated greetings, and excessive small talk when they don't serve the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example transformation shows trimming long, realistic 'hey' exchanges into concise lines that move the scene forward. Keep what is dramatic or revealing; drop the rest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make dialogue reveal character and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should give information about who characters are and the relationships/tension between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dialogue to show personality, dependency, and conflict (e.g., Gina/Dana exchange reveals dependence on Matt and a challenging tone). A few lines can yield a wealth of information if chosen well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to conventional quotation punctuation unless you have a reason not to
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks signal that someone is speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasionally authors use single quotes, dashes, brackets, or no marks, but unless you have a compelling reason stick with double quotes for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: One paragraph per speaker for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually dialogue dedicates one paragraph per speaker, no matter how short the speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights importance and makes it easier to follow the flow. Putting different speakers in the same paragraph can be confusing or intimidating to the reader; avoid unless purposeful and clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tags/attributions sparingly — 'said' is invisible and effective
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Said' is the most frequently used tag and becomes nearly invisible to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You could use nothing but 'said' and readers likely wouldn't notice. Though it may feel tedious, it helps readers gather bearings. Relying on 'said' avoids drawing attention to the tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant speech verbs and overusing synonyms for 'said'
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a thesaurus to swap 'said' for announce, proclaim, sputter, etc., can be distracting and seem forced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong verbs like 'sputtered' or 'proclaimed' can create a trampoline effect and make banal lines sound overblown. Reserve vivid verbs for truly appropriate moments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid adverbs in speech tags as a rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs in tags (e.g., 'she screamed stridently') tend to make the author seem amateurish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let what the character says and action convey tone; use adverbs sparingly because they draw attention and are often unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exclamation points in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclamation points tend to make written dialogue sound overwrought or adolescent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try at all costs to avoid using them; rely on content, rhythm, and stage directions to convey emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place tags logically; mid-sentence tags should follow natural breaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags should be placed where they feel natural and help the reader know who is speaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A jerky placement ('I don't,' she said, 'love you anymore.') is awkward. For long phrases, a mid-sentence tag is acceptable if it follows a natural break: 'I don't love you anymore,' she said, 'even though you still write me poems...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal speaker identity with names, actions, or thoughts when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Tags aren't the only way to indicate who is speaking; characters may say names or be linked to actions/thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lines like 'Hey, Pete, you got a light?' or combine speech with action ('Bert put down his coffee cup to stare out the window') or thought to show who's speaking. But be aware people rarely address others by name in normal speech; use sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can use sparse tags if speech voices are distinct enough
rubrics_metrics.description: With skillful and sparing use of tags, readers can follow multi-character exchanges without confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hemingway's 'Hills Like White Elephants' shows a passage with three characters where tags are minimal yet clarity is maintained; ensure voices and context make speakers identifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage directions and physical action enliven dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing narration details, gestures, and actions with dialogue gives scenes physical presence and reveals character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe behavior (gestures, mannerisms) and intersperse with speech. Actions can show character traits more imaginatively than telling (e.g., Gregarious people talk with their hands; nervous people laugh too loud). Use actions to show conflict between words and feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thoughts as part of stage directions when helpful
rubrics_metrics.description: Inner thoughts can be used alongside action to add nuance to dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoughts can explain discrepancies between speech and feeling or add an extra dimension, as long as they're used judiciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid too many stage directions — don't 'overact' the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Overdescribing every small action makes the scene feel overwrought and can drown out dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers do not need to know every shift of weight or mundane motion; excessive detail can prevent the reader from reaching the dialogue and make the scene seem contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use indirect (summarized) dialogue when the gist is more important
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect dialogue summarizes speech rather than quoting it verbatim; it can spare monotony while conveying essential information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize routine or lengthy back-and-forth and reserve direct quotation for especially significant lines. Mixing direct and indirect dialogue can be economical and effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give each character a distinct voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Every person speaks in a somewhat unique fashion; fictional characters should too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having all characters talk the same way or simply like the author. Look for unique speech traits, colloquialisms, grammar differences, and rhythms that reflect background and personality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary 'plentitude' of speech — balance verbosity across characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should differ in how much they speak: some may ramble, others may be monosyllabic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware extremes (endless monologues or constant grunts) that may frustrate readers; find believable variations that suit character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring pet expressions to characterize
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters often have habitual phrases that reveal personality (e.g., Gatsby's 'ol' sport').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pet expressions can efficiently establish voice; deploy them consistently but not to excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension between characters raises interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict or tension almost always increases the interest level of dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft exchanges that show friction, avoidance, or power dynamics; readers will hear the tension and be drawn into the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write dialogue with subtext — the unsaid meaning beneath the words
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtext is the meaning under the surface; characters often say something different from what they mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use miscommunication, evasions, and double meanings to create layered conversation. Ensure the subtext is clear to the reader (through context, action, or contrast) even if not spoken explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure poor communication serves a dramatic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion, evasions, and silences can be pleasurable and lifelike but should serve the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't include muddled exchanges or small talk unless the lack of clarity advances theme, character, or tension; aim for purposeful miscommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using dialogue as clumsy exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue is often a poor venue for dumping background or explaining facts characters already know.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a line feels forced because it conveys known information (e.g., 'You were six when your mother left'), rework so there is a believable reason the information is spoken, or place exposition in narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turning characters into mouthpieces for the author's argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Preaching or long political/social monologues from characters can feel manipulative and bore readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want to argue a point, use other forms (essay, letter) or craft characters and situations that naturally surface themes; it's very hard to pull off didactic dialogue without losing verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use profanity sparingly and strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: Written profanity reads as more vulgar than spoken profanity; overuse can alarm readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A couple of well-chosen swear words usually work better than a stream of expletives to convey flavor without overdoing it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle dialect carefully — give flavor, don't overdo or caricature
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialect is difficult: done carelessly it can be hackneyed, exaggerated, or offensive; done well it provides flavor without overwhelming the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on key words, speech patterns, and rhythms rather than phonetically spelling every utterance. Use 'less is more' to suggest ethnicity or region (Toni Morrison's measured use vs. Twain's full renderings). Avoid shoving dialect down the reader's throat.
